cues.zh: 废话不多说，我们开始吧。正如我所提到的，我们的第一个话题——将黑洞用作动力源——我们在之前的姊妹视频中已经探讨过了，当时讨论的是霍金辐射、

cues.zh: 微型黑洞，以及如何用它们为星际飞船提供动力。

cues.en: You may want to watch those or rewatch those before proceeding but the quick summary is that black holes are thought to emit Hawking Radiation loosely in proportion to their size, except backwards from what you'd expect. The giant monster sized ones in the centers of galaxies
cues.zh: 在继续观看之前，你可能想先看或重温一下那些视频，但简而言之：人们认为黑洞会发射霍金辐射，其辐射量大致与它们的体积成反比，这与你的直觉正好相反。银河系中心那些巨兽般的黑洞，

cues.en: emit so little of it that you'd need a trillion trillion years to collect enough energy to turn on a little LED light for a fraction of a second. Alternatively, the small ones gush out power so fast they burn out their entire mass in very short times.
cues.zh: 释放的辐射微乎其微，你需要花上一万万亿亿年收集到的能量，才能让一盏小LED灯亮起短短的一瞬间。相反，小黑洞喷发能量的速度极快，它们会在极短时间内耗尽全部质量。

cues.en: There's two upshots of this. First, that the lifespan of black holes is proportional to the cube of their mass, one twice as massive emits only a quarter of the power and lives eight times longer, one ten times as massive emits a hundredth of the power and lives a thousand times as long, etc.
cues.zh: 这有两层影响。首先，黑洞的寿命与其质量的立方成正比，质量翻倍的黑洞辐射功率只有四分之一，寿命却长八倍；质量是十倍的黑洞辐射功率只有百分之一，寿命却长一千倍，以此类推。

cues.en: Second,
cues.zh: 其次，

cues.en: if we can make artificial black holes, and especially if we can feed matter into them to replace what they lose to Hawking Radiation, we have an excellent power source for things. Black holes are roughly on par with antimatter,
cues.zh: 如果我们能造出人工黑洞，尤其是如果能向其中投入物质来补充它们因霍金辐射而损失的质量，我们就有了极佳的能源。黑洞大致与反物质相当，

cues.en: and vastly better than nuclear fission or fusion in terms of energy per unit mass of fuel and they don't blow up unless you starve them to death, a process that would take years or centuries normally making them a very attractive option for power generation and storage.
cues.zh: 而在单位质量燃料的能量方面，远远优于核裂变或核聚变，而且它们不会爆炸——除非你把它们饿死，而这个过程通常需要数年甚至数百年，这使得它们成为发电和储能方面极具吸引力的选择。

cues.en: Assuming we can figure out how to make small ones and feed them, both of which are actually a lot harder than with their bigger naturally occurring kindred, which again emit virtually no energy on timelines that can be measured without using scientific notation.
cues.zh: 前提是我们能弄清楚如何制造小型黑洞并为其供给物质，而这两件事实际上比对付天然存在的大型同类要难得多——后者在不用科学记数法就能衡量的时间尺度上几乎不释放任何能量。

cues.en: This doesn't mean we can't tap black holes for power in other ways though. The preferred way to tap a black hole for power quickly, which also works on neutron stars, is to suck out their rotational energy.
cues.zh: 不过这并不意味着我们不能用其他方式从黑洞中获取能量。快速从黑洞获取能量的首选方式，同样适用于中子星，就是抽取它们的旋转能量。

cues.en: Stars spin, same as planets, they have a lot of angular momentum and that is one of those conserved quantities in nature.
cues.zh: 恒星和行星一样会自转，它们拥有大量角动量，而角动量是自然界中的守恒量之一。

cues.en: When they die and collapse they start spinning much faster for the same reason an ice skater twirling around with her arms out will spin much faster by just bringing her arms in toward her body. Our Sun rotates around once a month. Neutron stars often rotate many times a second that is why pulsars make such handy clocks. I was going to say pulsars are a type of neutron star but all neutron stars begin as pulsars,
cues.zh: 当它们死亡并坍缩时，会开始飞速旋转，原因和花样滑冰运动员张开双臂旋转时，只要把手臂收向身体就能转得快得多一样。我们的太阳大约一个月自转一圈。中子星常常每秒旋转很多次，这就是脉冲星能当如此便利时钟的原因。我本来想说脉冲星是中子星的一种，但其实所有中子星一开始都是脉冲星，

cues.en: it's just that they have to be pointing in our direction for us to notice the pulsing and that effect diminishes with time. This isn't a video on pulsars so I'll just simplify for the moment by saying they emit two narrow beams from opposite directions and if you're at the right angle each of those beams will pass over you every time it spins around, which again is many times a second. They only do this for the first hundred or so million years of their lives and only about a tenth happen to line up with Earth so it is right to think of pulsars as a type of neutron star, it's just a type that a, is fairly young and b, is coincidentally aimed our way. Every neutron star was a pulsar for someone at some point. Science fiction loves to say you can use pulsars to get navigational fixes off of and that's basically true but you need a catalog of all the young neutron stars to do that properly.
cues.zh: 只不过它们必须正好朝向我们的方向，我们才能注意到脉冲，而且这种效应会随时间减弱。这不是一期讲脉冲星的视频，所以我现在简化一下：它们会从相反方向发出两束窄光束，如果你处在合适角度，每次它旋转一圈，每束光都会扫过你一次，而它每秒会转很多圈。它们只在生命最初的约一亿年里这样做，而且只有大约十分之一恰好对准地球，所以把脉冲星看作中子星的一种是对的，只不过这种类型 a，相当年轻，b，碰巧朝向我们。每颗中子星在某个时刻都曾是某个人眼中的脉冲星。科幻作品很喜欢说你可以用脉冲星来定位导航，这基本没错，但你需要一份所有年轻中子星的目录才能做得靠谱。

cues.en: And again it is only young neutron stars you can use for this as they slowly lose energy and cool with time, something we'll discuss a bit more in the second section of the video. Anyway, needless to say black holes spin too, and very quickly, and both them and neutron stars emit huge magnetic fields as a result, same as Earth does from having a giant molten ball of spinning metal in its core. You can tap that power, sucking energy from spinning magnets was how the first electric generator worked, the Faraday Disk, which was the precursor of dynamos.
cues.zh: 而且只有年轻中子星能这样用，因为它们会慢慢失去能量并随时间冷却，这点我们会在视频第二部分再讨论。总之，黑洞也会自转，而且转得很快，它们和中子星都会因此产生巨大的磁场，就像地球核心有巨大的熔融金属球在旋转产生磁场一样。你可以利用这种能量，从旋转磁体中吸取能量正是第一台发电机的原理——法拉第圆盘，也就是发电机的雏形。

cues.en: The disk slowed down as it leaked power as electricity.
cues.zh: 圆盘在漏出电能的过程中会减速。

cues.en: Steering away that black hole's rotational energy, which is a large chunk of its total mass energy, is thus a pretty attractive option, and there's various proposed ways of doing that. The Penrose process is probably the best known of them and relies on being able to remove that energy because black hole's rotational energy is thought to be stored just outside the event horizon in what's called the Ergosphere.
cues.zh: 因此，引导出黑洞的旋转能量——这占其总质能的很大一部分——是个相当有吸引力的选项，人们提出了多种实现方式。彭罗斯过程可能是其中最著名的，它依赖于能够提取这种能量，因为黑洞的旋转能被认为储存在事件视界外侧的所谓能层中。

cues.en: You obviously can't dip under an event horizon and suck energy out, but we can from the Ergosphere.
cues.zh: 你显然无法潜入事件视界下方吸取能量，但我们可以从能层中提取。

cues.en: There's also the Blanford Xenoget Process,
cues.zh: 还有布兰福德-兹纳杰克过程，

cues.en: which is one of the lead candidates for explaining how quasars are powered.
cues.zh: 它是解释类星体如何获得能量的主要候选机制之一。

cues.en: If you're familiar with quasars and how they are brighter than most galaxies, this gives you an idea how much juice a black hole can provide.
cues.zh: 如果你了解类星体以及它们如何比大多数星系更亮，你就能大致想象黑洞能提供多少能量。

cues.en: It also taps the Oglesphere for power and does it by using an accretion disk so you'd use this on a black hole that already had one or that you were feeding, we'll come back to that in a moment.
cues.zh: 它还能从奥格尔球层中汲取能量，方式是使用吸积盘，所以你会在一个已经有吸积盘的黑洞上使用这个，或者在你正在向其投喂物质的黑洞上使用，我们稍后会回到这个话题。

cues.en: You can also just dump matter into a black hole, it gains kinetic energy as it falls down same as if we drop a rock off a tall building. If you tied a spool of thread to that rock and ran an axle through that spool attached to an electric generator you'd get electricity,
cues.zh: 你也可以直接把物质倾倒进黑洞，物质下落时会获得动能，就像我们从高楼上扔下一块石头一样。如果你把一卷线轴绑在那块石头上，并让一根轴穿过线轴连接到发电机上，你就能得到电，

cues.en: and you could do that same thing with a black hole too. Of course if you drop that rock off the building you'd get less power than you'd expect because the rock is falling through air, slamming into air particles and transferring much of its momentum to them, actually heating the air up in the process.
cues.zh: 你也可以对黑洞做同样的事情。当然，如果你从楼上扔下那块石头，你得到的功率会比预期少，因为石头在下落过程中会穿过空气，撞上空气粒子，把大部分动量传递给它们，实际上在这个过程中加热了空气。

cues.en: This is how parachutes work, transferring all that kinetic energy into a wide swath of air as heat. It's not a lot, but if the object is moving fast enough, like a spacecraft on reentry, it's a lot more and can make the object and the air it's hitting so hot it will glow. You would gain some power with a solar panel that was nearby drinking in that light, and you can do the same with a black hole because as matter falls towards them and often ends up in orbit around the black hole rather than directly entering, it forms what we call an accretion disk, and those glow quite brightly giving off a lot of photons you can collect to use for power. If you dump matter into a black hole you can collect that power. It should be noted that when things approach large masses they usually don't curve and slam down into them, and that's as true for black holes as anything else. Their path curves, depending on how close they get and how massive they are. If they are very close to a very large mass they will hook right in, but normally they either fly off at a different angle or enter an orbit, and if there's other stuff hanging around there for them to bump into their orbit will decay and they'll eventually fall in. All that bumping, again, generates heat and if there's enough heat lots of visible light too, same as a red hot chunk of metal. That's an accretion disk for a black hole, and everything that falls into a black hole will add to its rotational energy too, though if it goes in backwards it will subtract from it. So if you're dumping matter into black holes it pays to drop in the right direction.
cues.zh: 这就是降落伞的工作原理，把所有动能转化为大范围空气的热量。这并不多，但如果物体移动得足够快，比如重返大气层的航天器，那就多得多，能让物体和它撞击的空气热到发光。你可以用附近的太阳能板吸收那光来获得一些功率，对黑洞也可以做同样的事，因为当物质向黑洞下落时，往往最终进入环绕黑洞的轨道而不是直接进入，这就形成了我们所说的吸积盘，那些吸积盘发光相当明亮，释放出大量光子，你可以收集它们来获取能量。如果你把物质倾倒进黑洞，你就能收集那份能量。应该指出，当物体接近大质量天体时，它们通常不会弯曲并猛撞上去，这对黑洞和其他天体一样适用。它们的路径会弯曲，取决于它们靠得多近以及天体质量多大。如果它们非常接近一个非常大的质量，它们会直接钩进去，但通常它们要么以不同角度飞走，要么进入轨道，如果周围还有其他东西让它们撞上，它们的轨道就会衰减，最终掉进去。所有这些碰撞，同样会产生热量，如果热量足够多，还会产生大量可见光，就像一块烧红的金属。这就是黑洞的吸积盘，而所有落入黑洞的东西也会增加它的旋转能量，不过如果是反向进入，就会减少它的旋转能量。所以如果你要把物质倾倒进黑洞，朝正确的方向投放是值得的。

cues.en: Now neither the rock on a string or the solar panels collecting light off matter dumped into a black hole is terribly efficient as these things go, but they are a lot conceptually easier for some than other methods I mentioned. Getting back to the Blandford Digenic Process, which as I said was a prime candidate for how Krasars work and another black hole power method and for our purposes it's pretty similar to the Penrose Mechanism but happens to have an equation you can use to determine how much power you get out of the thing. They aren't the same thing and if you want to explore the differences I'll attach a link in the video description to Sergei Komisalev's 2008 paper that details the differences for those who are interested. The equation shows us the power output of a black hole via this process goes with the square of the magnetic field strength of the accretion disk and the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole, both of which will rise if we increase the size of the accretion disk or if we increase the mass of the black hole, and in nature bigger black holes usually have much larger accretion disks. Particularly the big ones near the centers of galaxies,
cues.zh: 而无论是绳子上的岩石，还是收集落入黑洞物质所发出光的太阳能板，按这类事物的标准来看，效率都不太高，但对某些人来说，它们在概念上比其他我提到的方法容易得多。回到布兰福德双原动力过程，正如我所说，这是类星体工作原理的主要候选方案，也是另一种黑洞能量提取方法，就我们的目的而言，它与彭罗斯机制相当相似，但恰好有一个方程可以用来确定你能从中获取多少能量。它们并不是同一回事，如果你想探究其中的差异，我会在视频描述中附上链接，指向谢尔盖·科米萨列夫2008年的论文，其中为感兴趣的人详细说明了这些差异。该方程表明，通过这一过程，黑洞的功率输出与吸积盘磁场强度的平方以及黑洞的施瓦西半径成正比，而这两者都会随着吸积盘尺寸的增大或黑洞质量的增加而上升，在自然界中，更大的黑洞通常拥有大得多的吸积盘。尤其是星系中心附近的那些大黑洞，

cues.zh: 特别是活跃的年轻星系。

cues.en: As I mentioned this is usually considered a prime candidate for how quasars are powered and quasars frequently give off a 100 times the power of an entire regular galaxy. We would presumably want to tap that power a lot slower using much smaller black holes at matter flow rates. Now any of the methods that involve extracting rotational energy will eventually cause that black hole to slow and finally stop rotating.
cues.zh: 正如我提到的，这通常被认为是类星体能量来源的主要候选方案，而类星体经常释放出相当于整个普通星系100倍的能量。我们大概会希望以慢得多的速度、用更小的黑洞、以特定的物质流入速率来汲取这种能量。现在，任何涉及提取旋转能量的方法最终都会导致黑洞减速，并最终停止旋转。

cues.en: At that point while you can still dump matter in you won't get nearly as good a return and the black hole's mass will increase, making it live longer and giving off less power via Hawking Radiation, which is the only option I'm familiar with that lets you tap into the rest of that mass energy, as the black hole slowly evaporates,
cues.zh: 到那个时候，就算你还能继续往里扔物质，回报率也会大打折扣，黑洞的质量还会增加，从而活得更久，通过霍金辐射释放的能量也更少；而据我所知，在黑洞缓慢蒸发时，霍金辐射是榨取它剩余质能的唯一途径，

Not unless you can build ridiculously sturdy equipment that can operate without wear or tear needing power or replacement matter to fix over even more ridiculously long periods of time. But we will have at least a hundred trillion years to get better at building sturdy material

cues.zh: 或者准确地说，是目前关于宇宙自然老化与膨胀的主流理论。

cues.en: I mention that for two reasons.
cues.zh: 我提到这点有两个原因。

cues.en: First, that theory could be wrong, it probably is at least in part, or incomplete,
cues.zh: 第一，该理论可能是错的，至少可能部分有误，或者不够完整；

cues.en: and second, because we don't live in a Universe that's likely to continue along a natural path, because we live in it. Intelligent critters can change their environment after all, and generally tend to, and we've spent a lot of time on this channel talking about ways to tinker with planets, stars, and whole galaxies
cues.zh: 第二，我们生活的宇宙不太可能一直顺应自然发展，正因为我们身处其中。智慧生物终究能改变自己的环境，而且往往会付诸行动，我们在本频道也花了大量时间探讨改造行星、恒星乃至整个星系的方法，

cues.en: so it would seem silly to ignore how that could affect the progression of the Universe.
cues.zh: 所以如果无视这会对宇宙演化产生怎样的影响，未免就太不明智了。

cues.en: So first we have the Big Bang, which doesn't terribly interest us today, other than it being worth keeping in mind that the Universe began expanding then and continues to do so, and almost certainly has parts us so far away from us that we will never detect any light from them since new space emerges between them and us faster than light can cover the distance. This effect will only get worse with time and eventually only the galaxies in our local area close enough to be bound to us by gravity will remain.
cues.zh: 所以首先是宇宙大爆炸，今天它并不是我们特别感兴趣的主题，不过有件事值得记住，那就是宇宙从那时起开始膨胀，并且至今仍在继续；而且几乎可以肯定的是，宇宙中有些地方离我们如此之远，以至于我们永远无法检测到来自它们的光，因为它们与我们之间新出现的空间膨胀速度超过了光速。这种效应只会随着时间推移而加剧，最终将只剩下我们本地星系群中那些因引力与我们束缚在一起的星系。

cues.en: As those galaxies get further away and from all that emerging extra space seem to get further away faster and faster, the light from them redshifts and gets weaker and weaker. That's not the only red shifting light out though, and there's one type that is of great interest to us today for our final section. The Big Bang happened fourteen billion years ago, and just four hundred thousand years later an event called the Last Scattering took place. Not a long time, and I believe compared to the age of the Universe, but still a 100 times longer than recorded history and about the duration of human existence.
cues.zh: 随着这些星系渐行渐远，并且由于所有不断涌现的额外空间，它们似乎在以越来越快的速度远离，它们发出的光也会发生红移，并且变得越来越微弱。不过，这并不是光发生红移的唯一原因，有一种红移正是我们今天在最后一部分中极感兴趣的。宇宙大爆炸发生于一百四十亿年前，就在仅仅四十万年后，发生了一场名为“最后散射”的事件。这与宇宙的年龄相比并不算长，但我相信，它仍然比有记载的人类历史长了100倍，大约相当于人类存在的时间。

cues.en: That last scattering was an important event and is aptly named. Up until then the Universe was a much smaller and denser place, and small and dense means hot,
cues.zh: 那次最后散射是一个重要的事件，而且名副其实。在此之前，宇宙要小得多、也密集得多，而小和密就意味着炎热，

cues.en: very hot.
cues.zh: 非常炎热。

cues.en: Up until then the Universe would have glowed like a star in every single direction you look, a big white haze,
cues.zh: 在那之前，无论你朝哪个方向看，宇宙都会像恒星一样闪耀，一片巨大的白色雾霭，

cues.en: but the light emitted didn't go far because it was too hot for atoms to form yet and in that pre atomic plasma soup light scattered much easier.
cues.zh: 但发射出的光并没有传播太远，因为当时温度太高，原子还无法形成，而在那种原子诞生前的等离子体汤中，光更容易发生散射。

cues.en: As the Universe cooled down and suddenly atoms could form and were further apart from expansion,
cues.zh: 随着宇宙冷却，原子突然能够形成，而且由于宇宙膨胀，它们彼此间的距离也变得更远，

cues.en: photons could suddenly travel long distances
cues.zh: 光子也突然能够传播很长的距离

cues.en: without being likely run into anything and that kept plummeting.
cues.zh: 不太可能撞上任何东西，而这种碰撞的可能性也急剧下降。

cues.en: Most photons will never run into anything now. As a result there are always photons left over from them still flying through space thus far uninterrupted in their journey.
cues.zh: 现在，大多数光子永远不会撞上任何东西。因此，总有一些当年留下的光子仍在太空中飞行，至今没有中断它们的旅程。

cues.en: Now when they started off the spectrum was pretty similar to what stars emit, visible light, but over time as they traveled with new bits of space emerging along their path red shifting them, they've lost power.
cues.zh: 它们刚开始传播时，频谱与恒星发出的光非常相似，主要是可见光；但随着它们前进，沿途不断有新的空间区域出现，使它们发生红移，能量也逐渐减弱。

cues.en: They went through infrared and finally entered the microwave range just recently. This leftover radiation that's in the background of everything throughout the cosmos is called Cosmic Microwave Background Radiation.
cues.zh: 它们先经过红外波段，最近终于进入了微波范围。这种遍布整个宇宙、存在于一切背景中的遗留辐射，被称为宇宙微波背景辐射。

cues.en: As more time passes it will grow weaker and weaker and the universe will keep expanding and cooling. Eventually it will get so weak and cold that those bigger naturally occurring black holes will finally start giving off more Hawking Radiation than they absorb in the background radiation and actually begin to slowly age.
cues.zh: 随着时间继续流逝，它会越来越弱，而宇宙也会持续膨胀和冷却。最终，它会变得如此微弱和寒冷，以至于那些自然形成的大型黑洞释放的霍金辐射终于会超过它们从背景辐射中吸收的能量，并开始缓慢老化。

cues.en: Right now all naturally occurring black holes are actually growing in mass, even if there's no matter nearby to feed them. That time, when things are that cold, is a long, long way off. Before we get there we have our own Sun slowly getting hotter until it eventually renders Earth uninhabitable
cues.zh: 现在，所有自然形成的黑洞实际上都在增大质量，即使附近没有物质可供它们吞噬。等到宇宙变得那么寒冷，还要经过极其漫长的时间。在那之前，我们的太阳会逐渐变热，直到最终让地球变得不再适合居住

cues.en: and goes red giant, swallowing Earth, then leaves behind an Earth sized dense corpse called a white dwarf, which generates no new energy from fusion but still gives off lot of light compared to what our planet uses and ought to still be warm enough to light many Earths for even longer than its currently remaining lifetime before going red giant.
cues.zh: 并膨胀成红巨星，吞没地球，随后留下一个地球大小的致密残骸，称为白矮星。它不再通过聚变产生新的能量，但与地球的能耗相比，仍会发出大量光线，而且应该仍然足够温暖，能照亮许多个地球，持续时间甚至会超过它在变成红巨星前目前剩余的寿命。

cues.en: That's our first example of a civilization at the end of time because normally we figure it's the end of the road when our star goes Red Giant, at least here on Earth, and sooner than that too because the Sun is heating up and Earth will probably be uninhabitable inside a billion years.
cues.zh: 这就是我们第一个“时间尽头文明”的例子，因为通常我们认为，当恒星变成红巨星时就是终点，至少在地球上如此，而且还会更早，因为太阳正在变热，地球很可能在十亿年内就不宜居了。

cues.en: Except it won't, because there are intelligent critters on it. We may come back and explore this idea in more detail in the future but for now I want to use it as our first example of how you can't look at the timeline for the Natural Universe as particularly likely, not because the science is wrong but because it doesn't contemplate the impact of us on that timeline.
cues.zh: 但它不会，因为上面有智慧生物。我们以后可能会回来更详细地探讨这个想法，但现在我想用它作为第一个例子，说明你不能把自然宇宙的时间线看作特别可能，不是因为科学错了，而是因为它没有考虑我们对那条时间线的影响。

cues.en: We've talked a lot about moving planets or shielding them from light to cool them down. We looked at that in the terraforming video and more recently in the Ecumenopolis video.
cues.zh: 我们谈过很多关于移动行星或遮挡阳光来降温的内容。我们在terraform视频中看过这一点，最近在Ecumenopolis视频中也看过。

cues.en: So a billion years from now without intelligence Earth might be rendered uninhabitable by a sun growing hotter, but that probably won't be how it goes down. We might sterilize our planet ourselves long before that. Our track record when it comes to screwing up our planet on accident or blowing up chunks of it is not in my opinion quite as terrible as many naysayers think but it certainly isn't anything we want to brag about either.
cues.zh: 所以十亿年后，如果没有智慧生命，地球可能会因太阳变得更热而变得不宜居，但事情可能不会这样发展。我们可能在那之前很久就自己把地球 sterilize 了。在意外搞砸地球或炸掉它的一部分方面，我们的过往记录在我看来并不像许多唱衰者认为的那么糟糕，但也绝对不是我们想吹嘘的事情。

cues.en: Or we might disassemble it for building material. In the Megastructures series,
cues.zh: 或者我们可能把它拆解用作建筑材料。在Megastructures系列中，

cues.en: we've explored the basic idea that a planet, in terms of living area, is basically as efficient as a mountain with a few caves on it is. You get a lot more space by disassembling that planet to build megastructures,
cues.zh: 我们探讨过一个基本想法：就居住面积而言，一颗行星基本上和一座有几个山洞的山一样高效。通过拆解那颗行星来建造巨型结构，你能获得多得多空间，

cues.en: in the same way you would disassembling a mountain and its few cramped caves to use that rock and metal to build skyscrapers.
cues.zh: 就像你会拆解一座山和它那几个狭窄的山洞，用那些岩石和金属来建造摩天大楼一样。

cues.en: You could disassemble the average mountain and its cramped few caves able to hold maybe a few 100 and build housing for an entire planet.
cues.zh: 你可以拆掉一座普通山体，以及它那几个只能容纳几百人的逼仄洞穴，为整个星球建住房。

cues.en: Similarly, you can disassemble a planet and reassemble it as megastructures
cues.zh: 同样，你可以拆解一颗行星，再把它重新组装成巨型结构

cues.en: with thousands or millions of times the living area. So we might do that and have no planet here in a billion years.
cues.zh: 居住面积可达数千倍甚至数百万倍。所以我们可能会这么做，十亿年后这里就没有行星了。

cues.en: Or we could shade the planet, putting a large thin shade between us and the Sun, decreasing the light we got, especially the infrared range, which is pretty useless for plants, and keep us from burning up. Or we could just move the planet outwards.
cues.zh: 或者我们可以给行星遮阳，在我们和太阳之间放一块巨大的薄遮阳板，减少我们接收到的光，尤其是对植物来说相当没用的红外波段，并防止我们被烤焦。或者干脆把行星往外移。

cues.en: Moving planets is pretty time consuming as we discussed in the terraforming video but it is doable, requires no advanced technology, and we do have a billion years.
cues.zh: 移动行星相当耗时，正如我们在星球改造视频里讨论过的，但这是可行的，不需要先进技术，而且我们确实有十亿年时间。

cues.en: So in a billion years it would seem very unlikely the world will die, because it either will have long before us from us screwing up or using it for building material or because we valued it a lot and decided to preserve it. And you can protect against the red giant phase of a star and weather it and come back in to live around that white dwarf remnant for many billions of more years.
cues.zh: 所以十亿年后，世界似乎不太可能消亡，因为它要么早在我们之前就因为我们搞砸了、或把它当成建筑材料而消失，要么会因为我们非常珍视它并决定保护它而保留下来。而且你可以保护它挺过恒星的红巨星阶段，熬过那段时期，再回来围绕那颗白矮星残骸生活数十亿年。

cues.en: Of course even thirty billion years from now when that white dwarf is too cold to be of any further use to us, a black dwarf, the Universe will still be quite young and going full tilt.
cues.zh: 当然，即使从现在起三百亿年后，那颗白矮星已经冷到对我们毫无用处，变成黑矮星，宇宙仍然相当年轻，仍在全速运转。

cues.en: Our galaxy will still be forming stars at the same rate as now, only a bit faster since we will have merged with the Andromeda Galaxy by then and some of our other neighboring galaxies will have either merged in by then or be approaching.
cues.zh: 我们的银河系届时仍将以与现在相同的速率形成恒星，只是速度会稍微快一点，因为到那时我们已经与仙女座星系合并了，而且其他一些邻近星系到那时也已经合并进来或正在靠近。

cues.en: It won't be for another eight hundred billion years, about 200 times the age of Earth and 60 times the age of the Universe, and 200,000,000 times the duration recorded human history before the star formation starts dying off, and it will be an estimated one hundred trillion years before it ceases entirely.
cues.zh: 还要再过八千亿年——大约是地球年龄的200倍、宇宙年龄的60倍、人类记录历史时长的两亿倍——恒星的形成才会开始衰减，而据估计，要过一百万亿年它才会完全停止。

cues.en: There are stars that live longer than a trillion years and will still be around when star formation begins to ebb, and they are more efficient at burning their hydrogen to helium too, and we may look at some examples in the future of how creating stars or intentionally storing hydrogen in artificial gas giants or brown dwarfs might be used to similarly extend the lifespan of the star forming agent universe.
cues.zh: 有些恒星的寿命超过一万亿年，在恒星形成开始衰退时它们依然会存在，而且它们把氢燃烧成氦的效率也更高；未来我们可能会看到一些实例，了解如何通过制造恒星，或有意将氢储存在人造气态巨行星或褐矮星中，来以类似的方式延长充满恒星形成物质的宇宙的寿命。

cues.en: Or to create essentially compact Dyson Spheres high efficiency ultra long lived stars in what's been dubbed a Red Globular Galaxy, a sort of massive megastructure light years across that hangs on the edge of being a black hole even though it's not very dense.
cues.zh: 或者本质上建造紧凑的戴森球——即高效率、超长寿的恒星，位于被称为“红球状星系”的结构中，这是一种横跨数光年的巨型超级结构，虽然密度不大，却处于变成黑洞的边缘。

cues.en: To the best of my knowledge that's the largest continuous megastructure you can build, though I might be biased on it since it was my brainchild.
cues.zh: 据我所知，这是你能建造的最大的连续超级结构，不过我可能带有偏见，因为这是我的原创构想。

cues.en: Still we get stars for one hundred trillion years, and actually still some after that since even though the Universe will be composed of nothing but brown dwarves, white dwarves, black dwarves, neutron stars, and black holes, they will occasionally run into each other. And a white dwarf merging with a brown dwarf could form a new star as hydrogen is added to that stellar remnant,
cues.zh: 尽管如此，恒星还能存在一百万亿年，实际上在那之后也还会有一些，因为即便宇宙最终只剩下褐矮星、白矮星、黑矮星、中子星和黑洞，它们偶尔还是会撞到一起。而一颗白矮星与褐矮星合并，随着氢元素注入这颗恒星残骸，就可能诞生一颗新恒星，

cues.en: though if it is added too fast you get a Nova instead, a very common event in nature that never seems to get any mention compared to its much more spectacular big brother, the Supernova.
cues.zh: 不过如果氢加得太快，就会引发新星爆发，这种自然现象极为常见，但相比它那场面壮观得多的大哥——超新星，却似乎很少被提及。

cues.en: And the collision of dead stars is a common cause of Supernova.
cues.zh: 而死亡恒星之间的碰撞，本就是引发超新星爆发的常见原因。

cues.en: A whole lot of hydrogen hitting a white dwarf or neutron star or two of them slamming into each other is quite common since many stars are binaries and the bigger the pair will go red giant and expand to include its neighbor and cause that star's orbit to decay just like an accretion disk until they run into each other. So it's not just the explosion given off when a big star dies, kinda like the misimpression that pulsars are a particular type of neutron star. I think popular science and science fiction has tended to make folks think Supernova is synonymous with big giant star dying and nothing else.
cues.zh: 大量的氢撞击白矮星或中子星，或者两颗致密星直接相撞其实很常见，因为许多恒星都是双星系统，其中较大的一颗会演变成红巨星并膨胀吞没伴星，导致伴星的轨道像吸积盘一样不断衰减，直至彼此相撞。所以超新星并不只是大恒星死亡时引发的爆炸，这有点像人们误以为脉冲星是某种特定类型中子星的刻板印象。我认为科普和科幻作品往往让人误以为，超新星仅仅就等同于大恒星走向死亡。

cues.en: But that Universe, at the 100,000,000,000,000
cues.zh: 但在一百万亿年这个时间节点上的宇宙，

cues.en: mark, will be pretty dark and cold, and just keep getting more so. By then the other galaxies will all either have folded into our own or fled over the cosmological event horizon never to be seen again long ago. We'll still see light coming from them forever, but it will keep red shifting to be weaker and weaker.
cues.zh: 将会相当黑暗且寒冷，而且只会越来越冷。到那时，其他星系要么已经并入我们的星系，要么早就在很久以前越过了宇宙学事件视界，永不再现。我们仍能永远看到来自它们的光，但这些光会不断红移，变得越来越微弱。

cues.en: But we won't be able to talk to them anymore or them talk to us. The signal lag will keep getting longer and longer until it becomes infinite, and that will happen a lot sooner than the stars burning out. Indeed it's pretty much constantly happening all the time. The universe keeps expanding in size but the observable universe, which also keeps expanding in size, is constantly hemorrhaging mass over the horizon.
cues.zh: 但我们再也无法与他们交谈，他们也再也无法与我们交谈。信号延迟会越来越长，直到变成无限长，而这会比恒星燃尽来得早得多。事实上，这种事几乎一直在不断发生。宇宙的尺寸不断膨胀，但可观测宇宙——它的尺寸也在不断膨胀——却一直在视界之外不断流失质量。

cues.en: Most the galaxies that aren't close enough to us to be gravitationally bound but close enough to be reached without faster than light travel could conceivably be colonized over billions and trillions of years to come, by us, or might host alien lifeforms we might exchange long, very delayed cordial talks with. So I nicknamed this phase the long goodbye because all the civilizations around will presumably be omitting their history and commentary on life constantly
cues.zh: 那些距离我们不够近、无法被引力束缚，但又足够近、无需超光速旅行就能抵达的星系，可以想象在今后数十亿甚至数万亿年里被我们殖民，或者可能孕育着我们能够与之进行漫长而延迟极大的友好交谈的外星生命。所以我给这个阶段起了个绰号叫“漫长的告别”，因为周围所有文明大概都会不停地发出它们的历史和对生命的评论

cues.en: and one by one the furthest ones away would disappear, and you from them, and you know when it was coming so you could send out one last message to them. It probably would be culture chat and thus probably a sad goodbye since if you haven't invented some form of faster than light travel by then it's not like you have anything to fight over since you can't.
cues.zh: 然后最远的那些会一个接一个地消失，你从它们的视野中消失，而你知道这一刻何时到来，所以你能向他们发出最后一条消息。那大概会是文化闲聊，因此大概率是悲伤的告别，因为如果到那时你还没发明某种形式的超光速旅行，那也不像你有什么可争的，因为你争不了。

cues.en: I don't even think the most determined war monger will spend a billion years flying off to do war with someone, and it would seem if you haven't figured out how to go faster than light by then or beat entropy that you might as well settle in for the end. Though as we'll see it doesn't have to be the end and the speed of light actually becomes an increasingly smaller hindrance as time rolls on, even though the Universe keeps getting bigger.
cues.zh: 我甚至不认为最好战的战争贩子会花十亿年飞去跟谁打仗，而且看起来，如果到那时你还没搞明白怎么超光速或者战胜熵，那你不如安顿下来迎接终结。不过正如我们将看到的，它不一定就是终结，而且随着时间推移，光速实际上会变成越来越小的障碍，尽管宇宙一直在变大。

cues.en: So on to part three, Black Hole Farming.
cues.zh: 那么进入第三部分：黑洞农场。

cues.en: The Universe is a 100,000,000,000,000 years old, and now you're living on of hydrogen you've collected to either run-in artificial fusion reactors or make new stars from, or to feed into dead stars for a bit more power as you collect their slowly decreasing heat and light, or your artificial small black holes are running out of fuel if you've got them.
